prompt: China joined the World Trade Organization in:
explanation: China joined the WTO on December 11, 2001, after 15 years of negotiations. Integration into the global trading system accelerated China's export-led growth dramatically. The WTO itself was founded in 1995. China's WTO accession was a pivotal moment: it locked in China's role as the world's factory and contributed to manufacturing job losses in the US and Europe — a major political grievance that helped fuel populism in the 2010s.

prompt: The September 11, 2001 attacks were carried out by:
correctAnswer: Al-Qaeda
explanation: Al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden and based in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, planned and executed the 9/11 attacks. The Taliban was the Afghan government that hosted al-Qaeda but did not plan the attacks. ISIS (Islamic State) did not exist until years later; the claim of Iraqi government involvement was used to justify the 2003 Iraq War but was false. Bin Laden was killed by US Navy SEALs in Abbottabad, Pakistan on May 2, 2011.

prompt: India's economic liberalization in 1991 was led by Finance Minister:
correctAnswer: Manmohan Singh
explanation: Manmohan Singh, as Finance Minister under PM Narasimha Rao, oversaw the 1991 reforms that ended India's decades of 'License Raj' — a system of pervasive state controls on business. Facing a balance of payments crisis, India liberalized trade, welcomed foreign investment, and deregulated industries. Singh later became Prime Minister (2004–2014). The reforms sparked India's IT and services sector boom, though inequality and rural poverty remained significant challenges.

prompt: Between 1980 and 2020, China's economic reforms lifted approximately _________ million people out of extreme poverty — the largest poverty reduction in human history.
explanation: The World Bank estimates that China accounted for roughly 70% of global poverty reduction between 1990 and 2015. Starting from a per-capita GDP of around $300 in 1980, China's growth — approximately 9% annually for four decades — raised living standards dramatically. This achievement occurred under authoritarian political control, complicating simple narratives about the relationship between democracy and development.

prompt: Match each post-Cold War development to its approximate year:
explanation: These three events together shaped the early 21st century's geopolitics. The WTO institutionalized a globalized trade order; 9/11 triggered a global security paradigm shift; the Iraq War destabilized the Middle East with consequences still playing out today. All three are interconnected: globalization created economic grievances that fed extremism; 9/11 enabled a securitization of politics that justified the Iraq invasion; the Iraq War's failure contributed to ISIS and mass migration.

prompt: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at:
correctAnswer: CERN
explanation: Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, invented the Web at CERN (the European particle physics laboratory in Geneva) to help physicists share information. He proposed a system of hypertext documents accessible via the internet. He gave the Web to humanity without patenting it — a decision that arguably made him the most consequential uncompensated inventor in history. He later founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) to maintain open web standards.

prompt: The iPhone, which put the internet in most people's pockets, was first released in:
explanation: Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone on January 9, 2007, describing it as 'an iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator.' The smartphone revolution it launched transformed social media, navigation, photography, commerce, banking, and political mobilization. By 2023 there were roughly 6.8 billion smartphone subscriptions worldwide, though unique users were fewer because many people have more than one. No consumer technology in history diffused more rapidly or more thoroughly.

prompt: The Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018) revealed that data from how many Facebook users had been harvested without consent?
correctAnswer: 87 million
explanation: Cambridge Analytica, a political data firm, obtained data on approximately 87 million Facebook users through a personality quiz app that harvested not just respondents' data but all their friends' data too — without their knowledge. This data was used to build psychological profiles for targeted political advertising, including for the Trump 2016 campaign. The scandal broke weeks before the EU's GDPR (adopted in 2016) took effect in May 2018, and fed a wave of regulatory scrutiny.

prompt: ChatGPT, the large language model that introduced millions to generative AI, was released publicly in November ________.
explanation: OpenAI released ChatGPT on November 30, 2022. It reached one million users in 5 days and 100 million users in 2 months, at the time the fastest consumer technology adoption ever recorded. The release accelerated AI investment, competition, and public debate about AI safety, copyright, labor displacement, and regulation. GPT-4 followed in March 2023; competing models from Google (Gemini), Meta (Llama), and Anthropic (Claude) launched in rapid succession.

prompt: Match each digital platform to its founding year:
explanation: Google, Wikipedia, and Facebook each revolutionized how humanity accesses and shares information. Google organized the web through search; Wikipedia created a free, collaborative encyclopedia (now the fifth most visited website, in 334 languages); Facebook created social networking at scale. All three were founded within six years of each other — a burst of innovation comparable to the flowering of Renaissance Florence. All three also generated significant unintended consequences alongside their enormous benefits.

prompt: The Paris Agreement (2015) aimed to limit global temperature rise to:
options: Any level, provided emissions peaked by 2050
correctAnswer: 1.5–2°C above pre-industrial levels
explanation: The Paris Agreement set a target of limiting warming to 'well below 2°C' and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. As of 2024, the world has already warmed approximately 1.2°C, and current policies put us on track for 2.5–3°C. The 1.5°C target is widely considered likely to be breached in the 2030s. The Agreement is voluntary — nations set their own 'nationally determined contributions' — which critics argue makes it structurally insufficient.

prompt: Wangari Maathai's Green Belt Movement (Kenya, founded 1977) combined environmental restoration with:
options: Women's political organizing and community empowerment
correctAnswer: Women's political organizing and community empowerment
explanation: Maathai's genius was connecting tree planting — which restored degraded land and provided fuel and food — with women's organization and political consciousness. The Green Belt Movement planted 51 million trees and trained 30,000 women. Maathai was jailed and beaten by the Kenyan government; she persisted and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 — the first African woman and first environmentalist to do so. Her movement demonstrated that environmental and social justice are inseparable.

prompt: Between 2010 and 2020, the cost of solar photovoltaic power fell by approximately:
explanation: Solar PV costs fell roughly 90% between 2010 and 2020 — a steeper price decline than any energy technology in history. This 'learning curve' (sometimes called Swanson's Law) continued: by 2023, utility-scale solar was the cheapest source of new electricity generation in most countries. This economic transformation happened largely without notice in mainstream political debate, even as it fundamentally changed the feasibility of the energy transition.

prompt: The mRNA vaccine technology used in COVID-19 vaccines was pioneered by scientist Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman. Karikó won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in ________.
explanation: Karikó spent decades working on mRNA technology, repeatedly denied grants and demoted by her university because colleagues thought mRNA was a dead end. Her collaboration with Weissman at the University of Pennsylvania produced the key modification — pseudouridine substitution — that made mRNA stable enough for therapeutic use. Their work made the COVID vaccines possible. The Nobel committee's 2023 award recognized that their foundational discovery saved millions of lives.

prompt: Match each climate milestone to its year:
explanation: Climate governance has advanced incrementally over nearly 40 years, but emissions have continued rising throughout. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding targets only for developed countries; the US Senate never ratified it; the US withdrew in 2001. The Paris Agreement (2015) was more inclusive but voluntary. The gap between scientific urgency and political action is the defining tension of climate politics — and a case study in the difficulty of addressing long-horizon collective action problems.

prompt: Lehman Brothers' collapse on September 15, 2008 triggered:
options: A local US banking crisis that was quickly contained
A global credit freeze and the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression
The start of the Eurozone crisis only
A brief stock market correction that recovered within months
correctAnswer: A global credit freeze and the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression
explanation: Lehman Brothers was the fourth-largest US investment bank. Its bankruptcy — the largest in US history at the time — froze global credit markets overnight. Banks stopped lending to each other; businesses could not access payroll financing; trade finance collapsed. Global GDP fell in 2009 for the first time since World War II. Governments injected trillions in bailouts and stimulus. Recovery was slow and uneven; austerity policies imposed in Europe prolonged unemployment and fed political extremism.

prompt: Brexit refers to:
options: The United Kingdom's vote to leave the European Union in 2016
The UK's departure from the Commonwealth
correctAnswer: The United Kingdom's vote to leave the European Union in 2016
explanation: On June 23, 2016, the UK voted 52%–48% to leave the EU. The 'Leave' campaign promised sovereignty, control of immigration, and £350 million per week for the NHS (a claim later admitted to be misleading). The UK formally left the EU on January 31, 2020. Brexit's economic consequences — reduced trade, staff shortages in healthcare and hospitality, financial sector relocation — have been significant and remain politically contested.

prompt: Vladimir Putin described the collapse of the Soviet Union as:
options: The greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century
A victory for the Russian people
correctAnswer: The greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century
explanation: Putin made this statement in his 2005 State of the Nation address. It signaled a fundamental break from the post-Cold War assumption that Russia had accepted Western-led liberal order as legitimate. Putin's subsequent actions — the assertion of Russian 'spheres of influence,' the invasion of Georgia (2008), the annexation of Crimea (2014), and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine (2022) — can be understood as attempts to reverse what he characterized as a catastrophe.

prompt: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, _________, triggering Europe's largest military conflict since World War II.
explanation: Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022 followed the 2014 annexation of Crimea and the war in the Donbas. The invasion prompted the largest Western sanctions regime in history, massive military aid to Ukraine, and a NATO enlargement (Finland and Sweden joined). The war reshaped European security, accelerated the energy transition away from Russian gas, and created a global food crisis as Ukraine is a major grain exporter.

prompt: Match each 21st-century populist development to its country:
explanation: Populism's 21st-century wave crossed left-right boundaries and national contexts. Brexit, Orbán, and Bolsonaro all combined anti-elite rhetoric with nationalist identity politics, opposition to liberal media, and hostility to international institutions. Each had different outcomes: Brexit was implemented despite severe economic costs; Orbán consolidated one-party control; Bolsonaro lost the 2022 election to Lula da Silva and was later convicted (2025) of plotting a coup to stay in power. Comparing cases helps identify what is structural versus contingent in democratic backsliding.

prompt: The COVID-19 pandemic's mRNA vaccines were notable because:
options: They were developed in under one year — the fastest vaccine development in history
correctAnswer: They were developed in under one year — the fastest vaccine development in history
explanation: The COVID vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna) went from genetic sequence to emergency authorization in under 12 months — previous vaccines had taken 4–20 years. This was possible because: regulatory pathways were expedited (without cutting safety corners); mRNA technology had been developed over 30 years; massive funding removed financial barriers; and clinical trials ran in parallel rather than sequentially. Karikó and Weissman's foundational mRNA work won the 2023 Nobel Prize.

prompt: Greta Thunberg began her school climate strike outside the Swedish parliament in:
explanation: Thunberg began her 'Skolstrejk för klimatet' (school strike for climate) strike outside the Riksdag in August 2018, aged 15, ahead of Swedish elections. She continued striking every Friday, inspiring the global Fridays for Future movement. By September 2019, over 7.6 million people in 161 countries participated in a global climate strike. Her address to the UN ('How dare you!') went viral globally. She became a lightning rod: celebrated by climate advocates, attacked by fossil fuel interests and right-wing politicians.

prompt: The global Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 were triggered by:
options: The police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis on May 25, 2020
The shooting at a Charleston church
correctAnswer: The police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis on May 25, 2020
explanation: George Floyd's murder by Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin — filmed by bystanders and shared globally — triggered protests in over 2,000 US cities and dozens of countries. It was the largest protest movement in US history by number of participants (estimated 15–26 million). Chauvin was convicted of murder in April 2021. The movement reinvigorated debates about policing, racial justice, and institutional reform, while also producing a political backlash that shaped subsequent elections.

prompt: Shoshana Zuboff popularized the term '_________ capitalism' to describe the business model of tracking human behavior as raw material for behavioral prediction products sold to advertisers.
correctAnswer: surveillance
explanation: Zuboff's 'The Age of Surveillance Capitalism' (2019) argued that companies like Google and Facebook had developed a new economic logic: human experience — clicks, location, relationships, emotions — is harvested as free raw material, processed into predictions of future behavior, and sold to advertisers. This monetizes not just data but behavioral modification. Zuboff argues this represents a new form of power distinct from industrial capitalism, with profound implications for democracy and human autonomy.

prompt: Match each 21st-century social movement to its primary cause:

pairs.right: Racial justice and police violence against Black people

explanation: These three movements share structural features: all were amplified by social media; all were sparked by specific incidents (Weinstein revelations, Trayvon Martin's killing, Thunberg's personal protest); all achieved significant cultural and sometimes policy impact; and all generated significant backlash. Studying them together reveals patterns in how 21st-century social movements form, spread, and succeed or fail. They also demonstrate how technology changes the calculus of collective action.

prompt: HIV originated as:
options: A virus that crossed from chimpanzees to humans in west-central Africa, spreading silently for decades before global awareness in the 1980s
correctAnswer: A virus that crossed from chimpanzees to humans in west-central Africa, spreading silently for decades before global awareness in the 1980s
explanation: Modern HIV-1 likely jumped from chimpanzees ~1920s. Spread quietly in central Africa, then globally with travel patterns. Killed ~40 million people total; ~40 million currently live with HIV.

prompt: What transformed HIV from a death sentence into a manageable chronic condition?
correctAnswer: Antiretroviral therapy (combination drug regimens, from 1996)
explanation: ART suppresses viral replication. People on effective treatment have near-normal life expectancy and don't transmit HIV to partners. PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) prevents new infections in at-risk people.

prompt: COVID-19 vaccines based on mRNA technology:
options: Were designed within days of viral genome release and deployed at scale within ~11 months — record fast
correctAnswer: Were designed within days of viral genome release and deployed at scale within ~11 months — record fast
explanation: Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna mRNA vaccines were designed in January 2020, after SARS-CoV-2 sequence release. Phase 3 trials and emergency use authorization by December 2020. Saved millions of lives. Demonstrated mRNA platform's potential.

prompt: COVID-19's true global death toll, including excess mortality, is likely 15-20+ million.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: Confirmed deaths ~7M; excess mortality estimates run higher. Some countries undercount; some pandemic-related deaths weren't directly from COVID. The pandemic was the deadliest in over a century.

prompt: Match each pandemic/health concept to its description:

pairs.right: Chimpanzee-origin virus, ~40M deaths, manageable with ART
Looming public health crisis as antibiotics fail

explanation: 21st-century health challenges include both new threats (novel viruses, AMR) and old ones (HIV continues; pandemic response remains underprepared). Climate change adds further dimensions.

prompt: What was AlexNet's significance (2012)?
options: Deep neural network won ImageNet competition by a huge margin, sparking the deep-learning revolution
correctAnswer: Deep neural network won ImageNet competition by a huge margin, sparking the deep-learning revolution
explanation: AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton) used GPUs to train a convolutional neural network. Computer vision's accuracy improved overnight. Triggered massive AI investment and the deep-learning era.

prompt: ChatGPT's launch (November 2022):
options: Was (at the time) the fastest-growing consumer app in history, reaching 100M users in two months
correctAnswer: Was (at the time) the fastest-growing consumer app in history, reaching 100M users in two months
explanation: Brought large language models to mainstream awareness overnight. Triggered massive AI investment, fears about job displacement, and recalibration of education and creative work. Fastest user-acquisition curve of any consumer technology up to then.

prompt: Modern AI infrastructure has become geopolitically significant because:
options: Advanced chips, data centers, and energy supplies for AI are choke points; US-China tech competition centers on them
correctAnswer: Advanced chips, data centers, and energy supplies for AI are choke points; US-China tech competition centers on them
explanation: TSMC (Taiwan) makes most advanced chips; ASML (Netherlands) makes the lithography machines. US export controls aim to slow China's AI capabilities. AI infrastructure is now a major geopolitical concern.

prompt: Some leading AI researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton, have publicly warned about risks from advanced AI.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: Hinton resigned from Google in 2023 to speak freely about AI risks. Hassabis, Bengio, and others have signed statements warning of AI risks comparable to nuclear weapons. The 'AI safety' field has grown rapidly. Whether the warnings reflect real or exaggerated risks is debated.

prompt: Match each AI milestone to its year:
explanation: AI's recent acceleration is striking. Each milestone built on the last. Whether the pace continues or hits limits is the open question of the 2020s.

prompt: September 11, 2001 attacks killed approximately:
correctAnswer: ~3,000 people
explanation: World Trade Center towers, Pentagon, and Flight 93. Triggered War on Terror — Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003) invasions, vast intelligence and security expansion globally.

prompt: The 2003 US invasion of Iraq:
options: Toppled Saddam but failed to find WMDs (the casus belli); unleashed sectarian war and contributed to ISIS's rise
correctAnswer: Toppled Saddam but failed to find WMDs (the casus belli); unleashed sectarian war and contributed to ISIS's rise
explanation: Major credibility blow for US foreign policy. ~hundreds of thousands of Iraqi deaths; long counterinsurgency war; sectarian violence; ISIS emerged in the chaos. The invasion remains highly contested.

prompt: The Arab Spring (2010-12):
options: Toppled some autocrats but produced mixed results — Tunisia partially democratized, Libya and Yemen descended into chaos, Syria into civil war, Egypt regressed via 2013 coup
correctAnswer: Toppled some autocrats but produced mixed results — Tunisia partially democratized, Libya and Yemen descended into chaos, Syria into civil war, Egypt regressed via 2013 coup
explanation: Triggered by Tunisian Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation. Showed both potential and limits of revolutionary uprisings. Syria's civil war alone has killed ~500,000 and displaced millions.

prompt: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine (February 24, 2022) is Europe's largest conventional war since WWII.
correctAnswer: True
explanation: Hundreds of thousands of casualties. Has reshaped European security thinking — NATO expanded with Finland and Sweden, defense spending surged across Europe, and Russia partially isolated. War continues into 2024-25.

prompt: Match each 21st-century conflict to its key feature:

pairs.right: 20-year US war ended with Taliban return
Largest European conventional war since WWII

explanation: The 21st century has seen no global wars but plenty of regional ones. The 2020s saw renewed great-power competition (Russia, China-Taiwan tensions) reminiscent of earlier eras.
